full_statement: In classical pinwheel scheduling, each task $i$ has an integer period $a_i$ and a feasible infinite schedule executes one task per day so that task $i$ appears at least once in every block of $a_i$ consecutive days. The density is $\sum_i 1/a_i$. The integer-period $5/6$ conjecture says that density at most $5/6$ guarantees schedulability, and Kawamura has recently proved this integer version. Kawamura's real-period extension assigns each task a positive real period $a_i$ and requires that for every positive integer $\ell$, task $i$ is executed at least $\ell$ times in every block of $\lceil \ell a_i\rceil$ consecutive days. The open problem is whether every finite real-period instance with density $\sum_i 1/a_i\le5/6$ is schedulable under this stronger all-$\ell$ condition.
known_results: The classical Chan-Chin $5/6$ density conjecture for integer-period pinwheel scheduling is reported as settled affirmatively by Kawamura, using a reduction to finite cases and computer-assisted ingredients. Before that resolution, Gasieniec, Smith, and Wild verified the integer-period conjecture for all instances with at most 12 tasks and developed Pareto-surface methods. Fujiwara, Miyagi, and Ouchi study Kawamura's real-period extension, where each task with real period $a_i$ must be executed at least $\ell$ times in every block of $\lceil \ell a_i\rceil$ days for every positive integer $\ell$. They prove the real-period conjecture when the periods take three distinct real values and explicitly conjecture the full $5/6$ threshold for arbitrary real periods. Thus the integer-period problem should no longer be listed as open here; the remaining target is the real-period extension.

literature.synthesis: Kawamura's integer-period proof changes the status of the classical Chan-Chin conjecture: the clean remaining problem is the real-period extension. The all-$\ell$ condition is stronger than simply rounding each real period once, because it controls execution frequencies in every long window. Fujiwara, Miyagi, and Ouchi's three-distinct-period theorem suggests that the integer proof's finite-reduction ideas may extend, but arbitrary real period spectra introduce approximation and limiting issues that are absent in the integer problem. A solution must explain whether real periods can be discretized without increasing density beyond the $5/6$ threshold or whether genuinely irrational period ratios create new obstructions.

reviewed.ref: Akitoshi Kawamura, 'Proof of the Density Threshold Conjecture for Pinwheel Scheduling', arXiv 2026
reviewed.result: Proves the classical integer-period $5/6$ density threshold and introduces useful real-period ideas.

reviewed.ref: Fujiwara, Miyagi, Ouchi, 'Pinwheel Scheduling with Real Periods', arXiv 2025
reviewed.result: Proves the real-period $5/6$ conjecture when periods take three distinct real values and conjectures the full real-period theorem.

reviewed.ref: Gasieniec, Smith, Wild, 'Towards the 5/6-Density Conjecture of Pinwheel Scheduling', arXiv 2021
reviewed.result: Develops Pareto-surface methods and verifies the integer-period conjecture for bounded task counts before Kawamura's full proof.

agent_guidance.suitable_approaches: Study whether Kawamura's finite reduction for integer periods can be made robust under real-period perturbations. Search for discretization lemmas preserving the all-$\ell$ window constraints, and test irrational period ratios where naive rounding changes density or feasibility.
agent_guidance.verification_notes: A claimed solution must address arbitrary finite sets of real periods and the all-$\ell$ window condition, not just integer periods, rational periods with bounded denominators, or a single rounded deadline. A reduction from real to integer periods must control density and all window constraints uniformly. A counterexample must exhibit real periods with total density at most $5/6$ and prove that no infinite schedule satisfies the all-$\ell$ requirements. Computer-assisted finite reductions should include enough certificates to verify both the reduction and the finite schedule enumeration.
